name: Wins Above Replacement
summary: An estimate of how many fewer games a team would have won with a readily available fill-in, a replacement player, in this player's place.
easy: Hitting, baserunning, defense and the difficulty of the position all get converted into wins and added together. That's what makes it possible to put a shortstop and a designated hitter, or a starting pitcher and a closer, on the same list.

The baseline isn't an average player. A replacement player is the kind a team can pick up cheaply from the minors or the bench. A WAR of 0 doesn't mean average. It means anybody could fill the spot. The usual feel is that an everyday regular should be good for about 2 a season.

scale.note: Based on a full season of playing time.

deep: The general shape: take the runs from hitting, baserunning and defense, add adjustments for position, league and replacement level, and convert those runs into wins. Roughly 10 runs make a win, and that ratio shifts somewhat with each year's run environment.

WAR is closer to the name of a method than to one formula. FanGraphs' fWAR values pitchers by FIP, and Baseball-Reference's bWAR uses the runs they actually allowed. As a result, a pitcher who had luck on his side often has the higher bWAR, and one who didn't often has the higher fWAR.
Defensive metrics take a long time to build up a reliable sample. In a single season's WAR, the defensive share carries an especially wide margin of error.

myth.claim: A half-win gap in WAR settles which of two players was better.
myth.truth: It's an estimate, so it comes with error. Over one season, players within about a win of each other are safer to treat as roughly equal.

leagues.t: KBO WAR also differs depending on who calculates it, so the same player can come out with different values. When you quote a number, note whose it is.
